doc.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Jazz becoming elitist, like chamber music; rock and rap as alternatives
summary: Person compares jazz becoming an elite art form to classical chamber music for royalty, and argues people always find alternatives such as rock and rap.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Do you think that it’s because we have elevated jazz to almost a highbrow art form?

Yeah. It’s become an elitist — it’s become elite. A lot of people don’t really understand it you know. It’s a passing fad or diversion. But well it’s like what classical music became, and then classical music had problems, it became the same way. Even like in the, you © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

know like Ludwig in Bavaria. You’d have a composer write a tune and just his friends come to hear it. They’d sit there in a two thousand seat theater with about twenty people, his cronies would listen to it. The people couldn’t hear it. I don’t mean to call names, but this is what royalty did. They would give chamber music, and I guess that’s where “chamber” the term came from.
Yeah. Very small venue. And then that became sort of elitist. But the people will always find an alternate music.
If they’re not getting what they want, they’re going to go somewhere else.

Yeah. So when they couldn’t dance, they can’t rock. Rock ‘n roll and then they started dancing. Because you can’t kill the human spirit. They’ll find a way. The same way they cut music out of the schools, and bond issues and people wouldn’t vote to train kids, and then you had people just find a little turntable and they’d start scratching and making their own rhythm and then you’ve got rap. So the people will always find a way. And then you wonder why so many people like it — because they haven’t been exposed to anything else. You know, you keep it in the parlors. And it’s almost parlor music in some places.
